fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Built in Two Years or Already Standing?", "body": "Howdie Mickoski begins with the Chicago fair of 1893, 700 acres of Roman looking buildings said to have been raised in about two years and then blown up. He reports that a building contractor he consulted called that timeline impossible, estimating fifteen or sixteen years and 50,000 workers with modern machines. Howdie adds that construction photos from the 1904 St. Louis fair show scaffolding against finished buildings and no debris, which he reads as a cleanup of existing structures. He frames two options: technology we do not have, or an ancient North American civilization. Chance pulls up photos and urges listeners to explore them for themselves."}, {"title": "Money Trouble and the Fairs' Official Story", "body": "Howdie says the Philadelphia fair of 1876 lost four million dollars and that, by his account, no fair ever turned a profit, which strikes him as odd for wealthy backers. John asks where the money officially came from, and Howdie names the businessmen said to have funded Chicago, two bankers and a railroad baron, while noting a university project rising beside the fair. In his reading, the fairs, with their thousand page guidebooks, histories and symbol packed paintings, served as an official documentary of what the public should now believe. Before television and film, he says, they were the best vehicle for propaganda."}, {"title": "Howdie's Case That Humans Are Devolving", "body": "Asked by John where to put the goalposts between a rewritten nineteenth century and gradual progress, Howdie answers that humans have been devolving, not evolving. He says time at Egyptian, Toltec and Mayan sites convinced him that ancient builders reached a perfection of geometry and energy, and he describes feeling swirling energy in a cathedral in Nantes. Buildings made today, he says, feel dead. He recalls native medicine people telling him earlier generations were far greater, and he traces the idea of primitive ancestors to the fairs. Chance asks about Native cities; Howdie says he has no answer yet."}, {"title": "Reset Speculation and What Gets Forgotten", "body": "Howdie flags as research speculation his sense that a huge share of the world's population was eliminated between the 1820s and the 1860s, pointing to city fires whose photographs remind him of Dresden in 1944. Chance wonders whether falling fertility could be a slow reset, cites researchers who suggest Japanese could be extinct by 2200, and quotes Chrysostom on the vanished philosophy of the ancient world. Chance calls scant genealogical knowledge evidence of a reset. John adds the era's dislocations and schooling systems, Howdie adds orphan trains and ornate asylums, and in his outro Chance asks what else has been lost, given the unknown origins of astrology and tarot."}, {"title": "Columns, Universities and Grand Asylums", "body": "Chance shows his old college town of Columbia, Missouri, where by the official story a university building with massive ionic columns went up within nineteen years of the town's founding and was later ruined by fire, and he suggests anyone can find similar puzzles locally. Howdie says he watched such buildings vanish for parking lots in Ottawa and argues the columns still carry an energy people sense. Chance asks whether fair buildings became universities to control history, and Howdie points to the word university as universe city. John notes former asylum complexes near him, and Howdie says a hospital-turned-asylum outside Salt Lake City stood far from where people lived."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: What if everything we know about history is based on a foundation of lies? Was North America a continent of primitives, or a grand society with architecture and technology surpassing our modern capabilities? These are the questions on deck with Howdie Mickoski, an author, historian, and deeply spiritual researcher who wrote Exposing The Expositions: Ancient Rome In America?
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: Riding shotgun this time is John Coleman of the Apocatastasis Institute, bringing the perspective of history through academia and education.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Whose Story Are We Reading?", "body": "Howdie credits his history degree with one lasting lesson: before reading any book, research the person who wrote it, since the author's life colors what they present, and he asks listeners to apply the same test to him. He says university boxed in his creativity, and that John Anthony West's Serpent in the Sky convinced him the other Egypt books were probably garbage. John describes a maturation from rejecting a flawed system to discerning what is still useful. Later Howdie argues that nineteenth century Egypt scholars worked inside two camps, Bible chronology or evolution, and John says boxing off knowledge shapes daily life."}, {"title": "Is History a Simulation?", "body": "Howdie relays a paper mentioned in a recent conversation of his, which argues that a programmer would spend most effort on the present and future, so a past full of gaps and loose ends hints at a simulation. Chance offers a different reading: society can be simulated without any computer, because people and institutions repeat what they were programmed with, academia included, so history is something we simulate through belief. He suggests older cultures arose organically from attunement with nature, which is why old technology looks elegant and potent. John then asks Howdie for a narrative that fits the nineteenth century into earlier history."}, {"title": "Howdie on Buildings That Do Not Add Up", "body": "Howdie sees the Domus Aurea in Rome as a twin of the Chicago fair's main basin, saying it had no kitchens, bathrooms or bedrooms, and he rates the story of its Renaissance looking art being found by a boy falling through a hole as one or two percent likely. Chance cites a Barcelona hotel of 1888 said to have been built in 53 days for 2,000 guests. Howdie adds that, by his account, the St. Louis midway needed sixty or seventy thousand actors, points to a San Francisco photo of a cleared city weeks after the earthquake, and likens Soldier Field to the Circus Maximus."}, {"title": "Mud Floods and the Smithsonian Question", "body": "Asked by Chance to explain the mud flood idea, Howdie says he is fifty fifty on it, reads sloped streets and half buried floors as signs of digging out, and prefers to call it a worldwide destructive event with many forms of damage. Chance says he sees slanted, half buried first floors downtown in Springfield, Missouri. John asks about the Smithsonian, and Howdie offers his opinion that it works like the Vatican of North America, deciding what the public hears, and cites a reported 1909 Egyptian temple find in the Grand Canyon that he says vanished from the news."}, {"title": "Howdie's Energy View of Cathedrals and Art", "body": "Howdie reads from his book the proposal that cathedrals were energy machines, with towers and domes, copper and mercury drawing energy down and rose windows sending a cymatic pattern out, perhaps through organ music, and says Chartres matches only the pyramids and some Mexican sites for energy. Chance speculates that metal roofs might have shielded against frequency warfare, and Howdie adds chain mail as a Faraday cage idea. John notes the burst of thirteenth century cathedrals followed by the Black Death. Howdie then says ancient art existed to illuminate its viewers and tells of a Thutmose III statue he felt was breathing."}]
